input:
This energy assessment has been prepared in order to develop a comprehensive understanding of the way in which energy is used across a dairy plant, and to identify, from among the various opportunities that present themselves, the measure that offers the most compelling case for investment. The document is organised so as to move from the general to the particular: it begins with the current pattern of energy use across the site as a whole, goes on to examine the refrigeration load and the steam position in turn, and only then draws the threads together in a set of recommendations. It is in that final part of the document that the assessment's central proposal is set out, together with the figures on which it rests, and readers who are pressed for time may wish to turn to those pages first, although the reasoning that supports the proposal is developed in the sections that precede it.

## Current use
Electricity is the principal energy stream at the plant, and total electricity use amounts to 3368 MWh per year, a figure that has been assembled from the plant's billing records covering a full twelve months. The pattern that lies behind that total is a mixed one. On the one hand, there are the loads that are tied to production, which start and stop with the working day and fall away in the plant's quieter periods; on the other hand, there are loads, refrigeration foremost among them, together with standby and site services, which pay no attention to the production schedule at all and continue to draw power through nights, weekends and shutdowns. The total of 3368 MWh per year is used throughout this assessment as the baseline against which any potential saving is assessed, and it is worth emphasising that it is a full-year figure, since production itself varies over the course of the year and an average month, scaled up, would not provide a sound basis for comparison. It follows from the mixed character of the load that measures which operate only while production is running are inherently capable of less, over the course of a year, than measures which act upon the loads that run continuously, and this consideration has shaped the assessment's priorities from the outset, directing attention towards the largest loads and towards those which are present in every week of the year.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant, and understanding its character is essential to understanding the plant's energy position as a whole. The load arises in the first instance from the product itself: incoming product arrives above its storage temperature and has to be cooled down, and once it has been cooled it has to be held at temperature in cold storage for as long as it remains on site. Holding product at temperature is not a passive state but a continuous duty, because heat is constantly finding its way into the cold spaces, through the fabric of the building, through doorways each time product or people pass through them, and in the air that is exchanged at every opening. The refrigeration plant works against that ingress without pause, and it also serves chilled duties within the process itself. During the plant's idle periods, when production loads have stopped, the holding duty remains, and it is this duty, accumulated hour by hour across the whole year, that makes refrigeration the dominant load. There is a further point of considerable significance. Refrigeration is, in essence, the removal of heat, and the heat that is removed, together with the energy consumed in removing it, is rejected at the condensers. At the very same time, other parts of the plant are purchasing energy in order to produce heat for process and cleaning duties. The plant is therefore paying, simultaneously and continuously, to take heat out in one place and to put heat in in another, and it is this juxtaposition that the assessment's principal recommendation seeks to address.

## Steam
The steam position at the plant is a good deal less firmly established than the electricity position, and the figures that relate to it need to be handled with a certain amount of care. Steam is used for the plant's heating duties, which include bringing product up to process temperatures, providing hot water for cleaning operations, and holding temperatures where the process requires them to be held. The figures that were made available to the assessment were drawn from a single winter month, and it is important to appreciate the limitations that attach to figures of that provenance. In a winter month, ambient temperatures are at their lowest, so losses from the building and from ventilation are at their greatest; incoming product and water arrive at their coldest, so the heating duty attaching to each unit of throughput is at its highest; and even the water used for cleaning has further to be heated. All of these effects operate in the same direction, and the combined result is that a winter month's steam consumption is bound to overstate the consumption of an average month, to an extent that cannot be quantified from one month of data alone. The figures have accordingly been used in a restrained way, to identify the principal steam users and to give a sense of the shape of demand through a production day, and no attempt has been made to annualise them or to build savings calculations upon them. It should also be noted that, insofar as heat recovery might displace steam in any particular duty, that effect, while real enough, has not been quantified in this assessment and forms no part of the case that is set out below.

## Recommendation
In the light of the analysis set out above, the assessment recommends that the plant should proceed with a heat-recovery retrofit, and the figures on which that recommendation rests are as follows. The capital cost of the retrofit is estimated at $382k. The retrofit is projected to save 14% of the plant's electricity use, and, in absolute terms, that 14% equates to a saving of 472 MWh per year. When that saving is valued at $0.12 per kWh, it is worth $56582 per year, and the simple payback on the capital cost of $382k is therefore 6.8 years. A payback of 6.8 years is not, it must be said, a particularly rapid return, and the calculation is a simple one, which takes no account of maintenance costs or of possible future movements in the electricity price; moreover, the projected saving of 472 MWh per year, worth $56582 per year, is dependent upon the recovered heat being taken up throughout the year, although the continuous character of the refrigeration load, which is present in every week of the year, provides a sound physical basis for expecting that it will be. The recommendation is accordingly that management approve the retrofit, and it is further recommended that electricity consumption be metered following installation, on the same basis as the baseline, so that the savings that are actually achieved can be monitored against the annual saving that has been projected.

The assessment recommends the heat-recovery retrofit. It is projected to save 472 MWh of electricity per year, which is 14% of current use, at a capital cost of $382k; at current prices the saving is worth $56582 per year and the simple payback is 6.8 years. The case rests on refrigeration, the plant's largest electricity load, which runs continuously and rejects heat the plant can use. The steam figures in the assessment are drawn from a single winter month and are flagged as seasonal; they support no part of the saving figure, and the recommendation is built to stand without them.

## Current use
Electricity use at the plant is 3368 MWh per year, taken from billing records over a full year. The total is large enough, and the pattern of use steady enough, for electricity to be the stream on which the assessment builds its case. Production loads follow the intake and the production schedule: they start and stop with the working day and the working week, and they fall in the plant's quiet periods. Against them stand the loads that do not follow production at all — refrigeration above all, but also standby and site services — and these run through nights, weekends and shutdowns. The annual total is the sum of a variable part tied to output and a fixed part tied to the calendar. The distinction matters for any saving measure. A saving stated as a proportion of annual use is a claim about both parts unless it is restricted to one of them, and a measure that acts only when production runs cannot deliver the same annual figure as a measure acting on the fixed part. The billed total is taken as recorded and is not re-measured. Billing records state what was consumed and are the plant's own account of it; the uncertainty in this assessment sits in the savings projected from measures not yet installed, not in the baseline those savings are measured against. Production varies across the year, and with it the variable part of consumption; the baseline is therefore a year's total and not an average month multiplied up, and every saving figure in the assessment is stated against it on that basis.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use at the plant, and it takes that share by running rather than by drawing heavily at any one moment. Incoming product arrives above its storage temperature and must be cooled. Cooled product is held in cold storage, and holding is itself a continuous duty: heat enters through the fabric of the store, through doorways each time product or people move, and in the air exchanged at every opening, and the refrigeration plant works against that ingress without pause. Refrigeration also serves the chilled duties of the process itself, so the load has a production component; but its holding component runs through every idle period, and over a year the holding component is what accumulates. A load of this character has two consequences for the assessment. The first is scale: the largest single destination of the plant's electricity is a load that operates in every week of the year. The second is the heat the load rejects. Refrigeration is the removal of heat, and the removed heat, together with the work of compression, is rejected at the condensers. While that heat is being rejected, other parts of the plant consume purchased energy to make heat for process and cleaning duties. The plant therefore pays to remove heat in one place and pays to supply it in another, continuously and at the same time. Heat recovery intervenes in exactly that position. The retrofit takes heat from the rejection stream and delivers it to a duty that would otherwise be met from a purchased stream, and the continuity of the refrigeration load is what makes the recovered heat a year-round supply rather than a seasonal one. The projected saving is measured at the meter and stated against electricity use as a whole; the refrigeration load is named here because its size and its continuity are the physical basis on which a saving of that size exists to be made.

## Steam
Steam serves the heating duties of the plant: heating product to process temperatures, supplying hot water for cleaning, and holding temperatures where the process requires them. The steam figures available to the assessment come from one winter month, and the assessment flags them as seasonal wherever they are used. A winter month loads the steam system at its heaviest. Ambient temperatures are at their lowest, so fabric and ventilation losses are at their largest; incoming product and water arrive at their coldest, so the heating duty per unit of throughput is at its largest; and cleaning water is heated from a colder start. Every one of those effects inflates a winter figure relative to an average month, and they all act in the same direction. A winter month's steam consumption therefore cannot be annualised: multiplied up, it would overstate the year's steam demand by an amount the assessment cannot bound from a single month of data. The figures are used for the limited purposes they can serve. They identify the principal steam users, they show the shape of demand across a production day, and they establish that steam is a material stream in the plant's energy position. They quantify nothing beyond the month they were measured in, and no saving in this assessment is computed from them. If heat recovery displaces steam in any duty, that displacement is a real effect and an unquantified one; it is additional to the electricity saving on which the recommendation is based, and it is not counted in it. A full year of steam records, kept on the same basis as the electricity records, is what a quantified steam case would require.

## Recommendation
Plant management is recommended to approve the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $382k. The retrofit is projected to save 14% of electricity use, a saving of 472 MWh per year against current use of 3368 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh, that saving is worth $56582 per year, giving a simple payback of 6.8 years on the capital cost. The figures are stated on the electricity side of the plant's energy position only. The payback takes no account of maintenance costs on the installed equipment and no account of movement in the electricity price in either direction; it lengthens if the recovered heat is taken up for fewer hours than projected, and the take-up is the assumption the outcome depends on. The physical basis for expecting the take-up is the refrigeration load: it runs in every week of the year, so the heat is there to be recovered in every week of the year, and a use matched to it is supplied on the same schedule. The steam position does not enter the case. The steam figures come from one winter month and are seasonal, and the recommendation has been constructed so that nothing in it needs them: the saving is an electricity saving, computed from billed electricity and a stated price. Approval should carry two conditions, both of them cheap. Electricity use after installation is to be metered on the same basis as the baseline, so that the projected saving can be checked against the recorded saving. And steam use is to be recorded for a full year, so that the steam side of the plant's position, at present the unquantified side, can be stated on evidence if the case is revisited.
